summary: The Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill was passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and awaits presidential assent. An earlier version passed unanimously at third reading in February 2024, sharply increasing penalties and criminalising advocacy; it lapsed unsigned when parliament dissolved before the 2024 election and was reintroduced in March 2025. Human Rights Watch had called on the president to veto the 2024 bill. President John Mahama has previously signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill, and reporting attributes the 2026 passage to pressure from religious leaders on him. The Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the legislation, with Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson holding that until there is presidential assent there is no act, and review deferred until the president signs; the petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options.
tangentialFactors:
A 2017 bachelor's thesis at Diaconia University of Applied Sciences in Helsinki surveyed 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana: most opposed decriminalisation or legalisation, citing religious and cultural reasons and effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

The National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education, an education-policy position adjacent to the criminal-law provisions above.
localsOnly:
Young LGBTQ Ghanaians are disowned by their families and communities and evicted from their homes. When a young person discloses a same-sex orientation or a non-conforming gender identity, families commonly seek conversion therapy from religious groups; it is reported to be administered in abusive and inhumane settings, and medical bodies warn that it is ineffective and potentially harmful. An August 2018 report documented programmes run by religious leaders, and a 2018 conference claimed that about 400 people had registered for them.

A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana at significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than their heterosexual peers. Anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and some deaths by suicide among LGBTQ people are linked to forced evictions, blackmail and violence.

Community infrastructure has been closed rather than provided. Religious and political leaders forced the LGBTQ Centre in Accra to close in February 2021, and the Accra office of LGBT+ Rights Ghana, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021 after opposition from local residents, religious institutions and politicians. Most LGBTQ groups operate secretly or online, and FOTHA-Ghana members use the dark web for safety. No supported housing or shelter provision exists.

The Solace Initiative provides human-rights-trained paralegals to defend LGBTQ people in court.
outOfScopeNotes:
No finding in the sources establishes Ghana's legal gender recognition procedure or document-change rules for trans people. The nearest grounded items are the 1992 constitution's definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman, with Article 39 emphasising traditional values; a 2017 ILGA poll in which 55% of Ghanaians said transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender; and the pending bill's criminalisation of crossdressing and of identifying as transgender.

No entry, visa, or immigration and airport screening rule specific to trans travellers appears in the sources reviewed, and it is unresolved whether the identification offence, the crossdressing offence or the duty to report is applied to short-term visitors as distinct from residents.

No enforcement record for the 2026 bill exists yet; the Supreme Court deferred review of the legislation until presidential assent, and the most detailed documentation of violence and police conduct available is the January 2018 Human Rights Watch report and its 2017 interviews.
